Environmental Injuries Chapter 211

Bites and Stings

Most arthropod encounters are local wound problems, but the ED danger pattern is anaphylaxis, severe pain/autonomic envenomation, progressive neurologic toxicity, or delayed hematotoxicity.

Board trap: the right first move is syndrome recognition, not reflex antivenom or reflex antibiotics.

Hymenoptera: Bees, Wasps, Hornets, Yellow Jackets, Fire Ants

Hymenoptera cause more sting-related deaths than other insects because allergy, not local venom injury, drives fatality. Honeybees leave a barbed stinger; remove it immediately by any practical method because speed matters more than scrape-versus-pinch technique. Wasps, hornets, and yellow jackets can sting repeatedly and are frequent causes of systemic reactions.

Local reactions cause pain, erythema, pruritus, and swelling. Large local reactions may enlarge over 24 to 48 hours and mimic cellulitis without infection. Mouth, throat, or periorbital stings need airway/eye caution. Anaphylaxis is treated with IM epinephrine, airway and circulatory support, antihistamines and steroids as adjuncts, observation, epinephrine autoinjector education, and allergy referral after systemic reactions.

Spider Bite Overview

Most spiders cannot meaningfully envenomate humans. The medically important board patterns are necrotic arachnidism from Loxosceles, neuroautonomic latrodectism from widow spiders, and rare regional syndromes such as funnel-web or armed spider envenomation. Do not diagnose every ulcer as a brown recluse bite; geography, witnessed bite, spider identification, and course matter.

Brown Recluse / Loxosceles

Loxosceles spiders are brown with a violin-shaped marking and six eyes in three pairs. The bite is often painless at first; local lesions can become firm, violaceous, blistered, and necrotic over days. Severe systemic illness is uncommon in the United States but children can develop hemolysis 24 to 72 hours later with hemoglobinuria, rhabdomyolysis, renal injury, DIC, and shock.

Diagnosis is clinical and often overcalled. Important mimics include skin and soft tissue infection, pyoderma gangrenosum, fungal/viral lesions, foreign body reaction, and cutaneous anthrax. Treatment is supportive: local wound care, analgesia, tetanus update, elevation/ice as tolerated, antibiotics only for true infection, and delayed surgical management after margins declare. Dapsone, steroids, colchicine, hyperbaric oxygen, early excision, and antivenom are not routine ED fixes.

Black Widow / Latrodectus

Black widow venom contains alpha-latrotoxin, causing acetylcholine, norepinephrine, and other neurotransmitter release. The syndrome is pain out of proportion: pinprick bite, regional or generalized pain, muscle cramps, abdominal rigidity, diaphoresis, hypertension, tachycardia, nausea, vomiting, headache, and sometimes priapism or myocarditis.

The diagnosis is clinical; there is no routine confirmatory lab. Treat with wound cleansing, tetanus update, opioids for pain, and benzodiazepines for muscle spasm/agitation. Calcium gluconate and dantrolene are not reliable routine therapy. Antivenom can rapidly improve severe cases but is equine-derived, may cause anaphylaxis/serum sickness, and should be reserved for severe persistent symptoms or high-risk patients after risk-benefit discussion.

Scorpion Stings

Scorpion venom produces immediate local pain and paresthesias; severe Centruroides envenomation causes autonomic and neuromuscular excitation. Concerning findings include tachycardia, hypertension, hypersalivation, vomiting, diaphoresis, abnormal eye movements, roving eyes, dysphagia, slurred speech, skeletal muscle jerking, restlessness, and respiratory compromise. Children are at higher risk for rapid severe disease.

Local effects are treated with wound care, ice, NSAIDs/analgesia, and local anesthetic without epinephrine when needed. Systemic neuromuscular or autonomic toxicity requires cardiorespiratory monitoring, benzodiazepines, opioids when appropriate, and Centruroides immune F(ab)2 antivenom for severe North American bark scorpion envenomation. Antivenom binds circulating venom but does not reverse established end-organ injury instantly.

Other Arthropods

Chiggers cause intensely pruritic papules or papulovesicles after outdoor exposure and are treated with antihistamines, topical steroids, hygiene, and infection treatment only when secondary infection occurs. Mosquitoes, flies, fleas, lice, and bedbugs mostly cause local pruritic reactions, but mosquito-borne disease history matters for fever, travel, and outbreak context.

Tick paralysis is a progressive ascending paralysis caused by attached ticks; the key treatment is finding and removing the tick, with supportive care until weakness resolves. Centipedes cause painful local erythema and edema treated with local care and analgesia. Kissing bugs and other arthropods may produce allergic reactions; treat by severity.

Drug Dose Reference

This section is only a quick recap after the full clinical treatment sections.

TherapyUseHigh-yield caution
IM epinephrineHymenoptera/fire-ant anaphylaxisUse early with ABC support; observe for recurrence.
Opioids + benzodiazepinesSevere Latrodectus pain/cramps or severe scorpion neuromuscular agitationTitrate with respiratory monitoring.
Latrodectus antivenomSevere persistent widow symptoms/high-risk patientsEquine-derived; anaphylaxis/serum sickness risk.
Centruroides immune F(ab)2Severe North American bark scorpion envenomationBest for grade 3-4 neuromuscular/autonomic toxicity.
AntibioticsOnly if secondary infection/cellulitisNot routine for clean bites/stings.

Inline Assessment MCQs

Q1. Most deaths from arthropod stings are from:

A. Hymenoptera anaphylaxisCorrect: bee/wasp/hornet/yellow-jacket allergy kills more than direct local venom.
B. Simple mosquito bitesMosquito bites are usually local; vector disease is separate.
C. All brown recluse bitesBrown recluse systemic toxicity is uncommon in the United States.
D. All tick bitesTick-borne disease matters, but not the usual immediate sting-fatality mechanism.

Q2. A honeybee stinger is still visible in the skin. Best next step:

A. Delay removal until forceps are foundDelay leaves venom apparatus contracting.
B. Remove it immediately by any practical methodCorrect: speed matters more than scrape-versus-pinch technique.
C. Inject lidocaine with epinephrine through the stingerNot the priority.
D. Do nothing because venom stops instantlyVenom can continue briefly after detachment.

Q3. Large local Hymenoptera reactions:

A. Always require antibioticsAntibiotics are for true infection.
B. Are proof of anaphylaxisLocal swelling alone is not systemic anaphylaxis.
C. May enlarge over 1-2 days and can mimic infectionCorrect.
D. Never involve airway riskOral/pharyngeal swelling can threaten airway.

Q4. Systemic Hymenoptera reaction in the ED should be treated first with:

A. Oral antihistamine onlyAdjunct only.
B. Topical steroidNot enough.
C. Observation onlyUnsafe for anaphylaxis.
D. IM epinephrine plus ABC supportCorrect.

Q5. Fire ant lesions classically produce:

A. Sterile pustules that should be kept clean and not openedCorrect.
B. Mandatory incision and drainageOpening pustules increases infection risk.
C. Immediate necrotizing fasciitis in all patientsNot typical.
D. No allergic riskFire ants can cause systemic allergy.

Q6. The brown recluse bite diagnosis is most reliable when:

A. Any necrotic ulcer is presentMany mimics cause ulcers.
B. The spider is identified in an endemic area with compatible courseCorrect.
C. There are many lesions all over the bodyNumerous lesions argue against recluse.
D. The lesion drains pus on day 1Early exudate suggests infection or another diagnosis.

Q7. Major brown recluse venom mediator of necrosis is:

A. Alpha-latrotoxinWidow spider toxin.
B. Histamine onlyToo simplistic.
C. Phospholipase D/sphingomyelinase D activityCorrect.
D. TetrodotoxinMarine/pufferfish toxin, not recluse.

Q8. Brown recluse systemic toxicity in children can include:

A. Only itchingToo mild.
B. Guaranteed hypertension onlyNot the hallmark.
C. Immediate flaccid paralysisTick paralysis/scorpion differential, not recluse hallmark.
D. Hemolysis, hemoglobinuria, rhabdomyolysis, renal injury, DICCorrect.

Q9. Brown recluse treatment is primarily:

A. Supportive wound care, analgesia, tetanus, infection treatment only if present, delayed surgery if neededCorrect.
B. Immediate wide excision for allEarly excision can worsen wounds.
C. Dapsone for every patientNot proven and has harms.
D. US antivenom for every patientNo routine US antivenom.

Q10. Black widow venom produces symptoms mainly by:

A. Local tissue necrosisRecluse pattern.
B. Massive neurotransmitter release from alpha-latrotoxinCorrect.
C. Blocking acetylcholine releaseBotulism mechanism.
D. HemolysisRecluse systemic pattern.

Q11. Latrodectism can mimic:

A. Simple cellulitis onlyToo narrow.
B. Stroke onlyNot typical.
C. Acute abdomen, renal colic, withdrawal, myocardial ischemiaCorrect.
D. Painless rash onlyPain and cramps are central.

Q12. Routine laboratory confirmation for black widow bite is:

A. Always available ELISANo routine test.
B. Required before treatmentNo.
C. Venom PCR from woundNo.
D. Not available; diagnosis is clinicalCorrect.

Q13. First-line symptomatic treatment for moderate black widow envenomation:

A. Opioid analgesia and benzodiazepines as neededCorrect.
B. Calcium gluconate as definitive treatmentNot supported as routine effective therapy.
C. Dantrolene for allNot recommended.
D. Antibiotics for allOnly if infection.

Q14. Latrodectus antivenom is best reserved for:

A. All witnessed bitesToo broad.
B. Severe persistent symptoms or high-risk patients after risk-benefit discussionCorrect.
C. Any itchy papuleNo.
D. Brown recluse woundsWrong spider.

Q15. A scorpion sting with cranial nerve dysfunction or skeletal neuromuscular dysfunction is Rosen grade:

A. 1Grade 1 is local only.
B. 2Grade 2 is local plus remote pain/paresthesia.
C. 3 or 4 depending combinationCorrect; these grades support antivenom use.
D. 0No.

Q16. Centruroides scorpion envenomation is especially concerning in:

A. Only healthy adults with local painUsually local care.
B. Patients with no symptomsNo.
C. Everyone needs intubationToo broad.
D. Young children and patients with systemic neuromuscular/autonomic signsCorrect.

Q17. Scorpion treatment for local effects only:

A. Wound care, analgesia/NSAID, local anesthetic without epinephrine as neededCorrect.
B. Mandatory antivenomSystemic severe cases.
C. High-dose antibioticsNot routine.
D. Immediate amputationNo.

Q18. Which scorpion finding pushes toward antivenom/benzodiazepines?

A. Tiny local wheal onlyLocal care.
B. Oculomotor abnormalities, neuromuscular agitation, muscle spasmsCorrect.
C. Asymptomatic exposureObserve if needed.
D. One healed puncture months laterNo acute envenomation.

Q19. Tick paralysis usually improves after:

A. DapsoneNo.
B. Latrodectus antivenomNo.
C. Finding and removing the tickCorrect.
D. Hyperbaric oxygenNo.

Q20. Chigger management is mainly:

A. AntivenomNo venom syndrome needing antivenom.
B. SurgeryNo.
C. No itch treatment allowedWrong.
D. Antipruritics/topical steroids, hygiene, and infection treatment only if secondary infectionCorrect.

Q21. Mosquito bite importance in this chapter includes:

A. Local allergic reactions and vector-borne disease awarenessCorrect.
B. Guaranteed venom shockNo.
C. LatrodectismWidow spider.
D. Hemolysis at 24-72 hBrown recluse systemic toxicity.

Q22. Best disposition after Hymenoptera anaphylaxis requiring epinephrine:

A. Immediate discharge after injectionUnsafe.
B. Observation at least several hours; longer if symptoms recur or severeCorrect.
C. No autoinjector educationAutoinjector education is important.
D. No allergy referral everSystemic reactions merit referral/immunotherapy discussion.

Q23. Black widow patient with no symptoms after observation can usually:

A. Receive routine antivenomNot indicated.
B. Be admitted for all casesToo broad.
C. Discharge with return precautions if reliable and wellCorrect.
D. Receive dapsoneFor recluse historically, not widow.

Q24. Brown recluse admission is most appropriate for:

A. Tiny stable local lesionOutpatient wound care may be enough.
B. No symptomsNo.
C. Mild itch onlyNo.
D. Expanding wound, systemic symptoms, hemolysis risk, or need for serial labs/wound careCorrect.

Q25. Rosen's scorpion table adds most directly:

A. A grading system linking Centruroides neurologic findings to antivenom decisionsCorrect.
B. A snakebite pit-viper algorithmDifferent chapter.
C. A pesticide cholinergic toxidrome tableDifferent chapter.
D. A frostbite staging chartCold injury.

Q26. Overall ED rule for bites and stings:

A. Every bite needs antivenomFalse.
B. Treat anaphylaxis first, identify the syndrome, control pain, use antivenom only for the right severe envenomation, and give clear return precautionsCorrect.
C. Ignore airway swellingUnsafe.
D. Use antibiotics for all arthropod woundsNot routine.
